title: The drug discovery pipeline
blurb: From target to approval: the long, expensive road a new medicine travels.
review: Stage timings are rough typical ranges; worth a check by someone in pharma R&D.

text.simple: Making a new medicine takes more than ten years and costs a fortune. Click through each stage on the left to see what happens.
text.student: Drug discovery runs through roughly eight stages, from picking a target to regulatory approval. Click each stage to explore it. [@hughes2011]
text.deep: The canonical pipeline: target ID/validation → hit discovery → hit-to-lead/lead optimization → preclinical development → phase I–III → regulatory review. [@hughes2011]

try.note: A knockdown experiment like this one is a classic way to ask 'is this protein a good target?'

text.simple: The playground is like the very first stage: you switch off a gene and see if the cancer cell cares. If it does, that gene's protein might be a good **target**.
text.student: Perturb-seq and other CRISPR screens are tools for **target identification and validation**: they reveal which genes a cancer cell depends on, and what happens when you remove them.
text.deep: Genetic perturbation phenocopies an ideal, perfectly selective inhibitor, which is useful for validation but optimistic: real compounds have off-targets, incomplete inhibition and pharmacokinetic limits.

text.simple: Here's the hard part: most drugs that look great on cells in a dish **don't work** or aren't safe in people. For cancer drugs, only about 3 in 100 that start human trials get approved.
text.student: A large study of trials from 2000–2015 found about **3.4%** of cancer drugs entering phase I were eventually approved, versus about 13.8% across all diseases. [@wong2019]
text.deep: Wong, Siah & Lo estimated a probability of success from phase I to approval of 3.4% for oncology versus 13.8% overall (2000–2015), with higher success for biomarker-selected trials. [@wong2019]

text.simple: Because so many drugs fail, the few that succeed have to pay for all the failures. Estimates range from about one to two-and-a-half billion dollars per new drug.
text.student: Estimates of the cost per approved drug, including failures and the cost of capital, range from about **$1 billion** to **$2.6 billion**. [@wouters2020] [@dimasi2016]
text.deep: DiMasi et al. estimated $2.6B (2013 USD, capitalized, self-originated compounds from large firms) [@dimasi2016]; Wouters et al. estimated a median of $985M using public SEC filings. [@wouters2020] Methods and samples drive the difference.

quiz.q: Why do drugs that work on cells in a dish often fail in people?
options: A body has many cell types, organs that process drugs, and an immune system that a dish lacks
Cells in dishes are always healthy
